analysis.one_liner: Requires big electricity suppliers to reach 70% renewable power by 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2021 with 26 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee vote or floor action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a federal requirement that large retail electricity suppliers generate a rising share of their power from renewable sources each year, reaching 70% by 2030. Suppliers would meet the target by earning or buying renewable electricity credits, with a $50-per-megawatt-hour penalty payment as a backstop. It also required a share of renewable projects to be small, local installations and to be built in communities harmed by pollution or coal-plant closures, and sent penalty money to states, at least half of which had to benefit those communities.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near fossil-fuel pollution, especially low-income communities and communities of color the bill defines as 'impacted communities', through reduced air pollution and a guaranteed share of renewable investment funds. Utility customers generally could benefit from cleaner air, and workers and communities tied to closing coal plants were named for priority benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Requires large retail electricity suppliers to reach 70% renewable electricity by 2030, with annual targets rising from 20% in 2021 [S2][S3].

Requires at least 15% (rising to 20%) of a supplier's compliance credits to come from small distributed generation, and the same share from projects built in 'impacted communities' — low-income areas, pollution-burdened areas, and communities hurt by coal mining or coal-plant closures [S3].

Sends suppliers' penalty payments ($50 per missing megawatt-hour, inflation-adjusted) to states, which must use them for renewable energy, storage, or efficiency and direct at least 50% of the funds to impacted communities [S3].
Directs regulators to prioritize community and public ownership of renewable projects and community benefit agreements [S3].
Clarifies that states may keep setting rates and incentives for renewable energy, protecting state clean-energy programs from federal preemption [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large electric utilities and fossil-fuel power generators, who would face compliance costs to shift generation to renewables; some of those costs could be passed through to electricity customers through rates.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for utilities would likely be recovered through electricity rates, so customers — including lower-income households — could see higher bills, even as the $50 alternative compliance payment sets a ceiling on the per-megawatt-hour cost of noncompliance [S3].

The $50 alternative compliance payment, adjusted for inflation, could in some years be cheaper for suppliers than building new renewable generation, allowing continued fossil generation while paying into a state fund [S3].

A federal standard would impose a single national mandate on regions with very different existing renewable mixes and grid conditions, a mismatch supporters of state-level flexibility have historically objected to [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit — a hard national schedule to replace fossil electricity with renewables and steer at least half the penalty money and a fifth of the projects toward pollution-burdened communities — is substantial and real. The main costs are potentially higher electricity rates during the transition and a design that lets suppliers buy their way out with penalty payments instead of building. On balance the public-health and climate benefits outweigh the compliance costs, but the penalty-payment escape hatch weakens the guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went straight to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the bill on June 16, 2021 with five original cosponsors, and 26 Democrats in total cosponsored it [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on June 16, 2021, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Energy [S5].
No further action was recorded: the committee never reported the bill, and the House never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Utilities and fossil-fuel power generators are better off because the bill died: they face no federal renewable mandate and no compliance costs, and electricity customers avoided any rate impact in the near term. Communities burdened by pollution gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Renewable Energy Act of 2021 on June 16, 2021.

for.name: 26 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral; no markup was ever scheduled
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 16, 2021 and never reported it out; the bill went to the Energy Subcommittee and no hearing or markup is recorded [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 26 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; the bill died in committee without any recorded opposition votes [S4][S5].

industries.note: A 70% renewable mandate by 2030 would shrink the market for coal and gas generation and force early retirement or retrofits of fossil plants. The bill's findings specifically target pollution concentrated in underserved communities, much of it from fossil generation [S3].

Utilities selling over 1 million megawatt-hours a year would bear compliance costs, though the credit-trading market and the $50 penalty-payment cap would let them manage or limit those costs; some costs would flow to customers through rates [S3].

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers (wind, solar, geothermal, marine, biogas)
industries.note: The standard creates a guaranteed, growing national market for renewable generation through tradable federal renewable electricity credits, with regional markets to spread projects across regions [S3].
A 15–20% carve-out of compliance credits for projects of 1 megawatt or less would create a protected market for community and rooftop-scale renewables [S3].
Only hydropower added to existing non-power dams after 2001 (with environmental protections) would earn credits, providing a new revenue stream for upgrades without rewarding existing dams [S3].
